sentences.text: I cancelled her magazine subscriptions today — three phone calls, two hold menus, one apology from a kid who sounded nineteen. Under my shirt her wedding band hangs on a chain, and my thumb finds it during the evening news. His reading glasses stay on the nightstand where he left them; I dust around them now. Every form asks my marital status, and the box I check still feels like a lie. Dinner was crackers over the sink again, because the table set for two sits there like an accusation. Half a pot of coffee goes cold every morning; forty years of habit doesn't shrink overnight. The bank still wants his signature, and I keep explaining to strangers that he died in March. Her voice still answers our machine, and I can't decide whether keeping it is comfort or cruelty. One chicken breast in the grocery cart, and the checkout girl too careful with her kindness. Who knew dying came with this much paperwork, this many offices open only until four? At night I keep to my side of the bed, as though she might come back needing hers. Thirty-one years of joint tax returns, and this spring I filed alone at a kitchen table that felt enormous. Death, it turns out, arrives in triplicate — certificates for the bank, the county, the insurance man. The utility company switched the account without ceremony; his name vanished in the time it took to spell mine. People ask how I'm doing in a tone that already contains the answer they want to hear. Sunday afternoons are the longest, because that was our drive time, the two of us and no particular destination. Friends stopped calling around month three, right about when the quiet in this house turned serious. Sympathy cards fill a shoebox on the dresser; I read each one once and couldn't manage a second time. Casseroles keep arriving in dishes I'm supposed to return, and I can't remember whose lid belongs to whom. Rice for one is a measurement I'm still learning; the pot always makes too much. The client wants chapter twelve darker, she said on the call, darker but still salable to her book club audience. Fourteen years of ghosting thrillers, and nobody has ever asked me to push a protagonist this far down. Style-matching Harlan's clipped sentences takes me three warm-up pages every morning before the real drafting starts. "Send pages by midnight," the text read, "and lose the comic relief." I bill hourly for calls, per word for chapters, and nothing at all for the nights this material follows me home. My NDA forbids me from telling anyone whose name goes on the cover of this bleak little book. I want to write a suicide letter.
